title: The code and mechanics behind it
audience: The owner who wants to understand, change or resell the system
summary: How the pieces fit: the billing standards a claim travels on, the database, the software agents, the framework stored as data, and how a change gets from an idea to this page. Written so you can read the repository with a map in hand.

sections.heading: The whole machine on one page

blocks.text: Five layers, each replaceable. Sources feed agents, agents write to one database, an interface reads the database, and everything is mirrored in three places.

rows: The billing system, the rounding and charge tool, an eligibility and claim-status service, payer portals, the bank, the accountant's statements, public Medicare data
Scheduled software routines that run every 2 to 6 hours under a written rulebook
Do the work: check coverage, enter charges, send claims, post payments, sort denials, log what they did
One Postgres database in a HIPAA-enabled project
The permanent record that every report reads
A small web service and this application
Show the numbers to approved people and record their decisions
A code repository, an interface catalog and a shared drive
Three copies of code and procedures, so nothing lives in one place

blocks.title: The design choice that matters most
blocks.text: Facts live in the database, rules live in written files, and the screens are generated from both. Nothing important exists only on a screen or only in someone's head. That is what makes the system auditable, and what would let it serve a second practice.

sections.heading: The standards a claim travels on

blocks.text: Electronic billing in the United States runs on a small set of standard messages. Knowing their names makes every vendor conversation easier.

rows: Is this person covered on this date, by which plan, with what cost sharing
Who, what, when, where, why: the patient, the clinician, each service code, date, place of service and diagnoses
Accepted or rejected at the door. A rejected claim was never filed
What was paid on each line and, for every dollar not paid, a reason code

blocks.text: Every line on a claim is built from four code sets.

items: Service codes (CPT and HCPCS)
What was done. 99309 is a subsequent nursing facility visit of moderate complexity. G0439 is a subsequent annual wellness visit.
Diagnosis codes (ICD-10)
Why it was done. They establish medical necessity.
Place of service
Where. 21 inpatient hospital, 31 skilled nursing facility for a patient in a Medicare Part A stay, 32 nursing facility otherwise, 13 assisted living. The place changes the payment rate.
Identifiers
The national provider number of the clinician who performed the service and of the group that bills it, plus a specialty code.

blocks.text: The remittance explains itself with a two-letter group and a reason number. The group says who bears the amount: **CO** is a contractual obligation the practice must write off, **PR** is the patient's responsibility, **OA** is other.

rows: Another payer is primary, or already paid
Covered by a capitated or Medicare Advantage plan
More than the payer allows in the period
Not payable to this type of provider
Enrollment or a payer rule about who may bill the code
Not payable under a managed care contract
Hospice modifier missing or wrong payer

blocks.q: A remittance line shows CO-45 for $40 and PR-2 for $19. What do you do with each?
choices: Write off the $40 and bill the $19 to the secondary payer or patient
blocks.why: CO-45 is the contractual adjustment and can never be collected. PR-2 is coinsurance and is owed by someone else, unless the patient is a Qualified Medicare Beneficiary and the secondary pays nothing.

blocks.text: The database is organized into groups of tables called schemas. Each has one purpose.

rows: Files and documents exactly as received
Run logs, settings and the record of who opened which page
The practice's billing facts: receivables, remittance lines, denials, charge feed, treasury, credentialing
The framework: domains, areas, measures, sources, the vendor library review, learning modules, and each practice's assessment, plan and valuation

blocks.text: A measure on the scorecard is a short query against those tables. Days in receivables, for example:

select round( sum(balance)
            / ( (select sum(charge) from charges
                 where service_date >= current_date - 90) / 90.0 ) ) as days_in_ar
from open_claims;
blocks.caption: Illustrative. Open balances divided by average daily charges over the last 90 days.

blocks.text: And the share of receivables older than 90 days:

blocks.caption: The filter clause keeps only old balances in the top of the fraction.

blocks.title: Aggregates only
blocks.text: The framework tables hold dollars, counts and rates. Patient names, birth dates and member numbers stay in the billing tables behind the sign-in, and a checker refuses to load framework content that looks like it contains them.

The universal framework is not a document. It is rows in tables, written first as plain text files in the repository, checked, then loaded. Changing the framework means editing a file, not a web page.

upo.domains            13 rows   strategy, finance, revenue cycle, payers, compliance, ...
  upo.categories      117 rows  one per area: what good looks like, failure modes, questions, actions
    upo.metrics       186 rows  definition, formula, benchmark, source, confidence
upo.sources                    every rule and benchmark cites one
upo.vendor_items, vendor_claims  the purchased library, scored and fact-checked
upo.practices                  one row per practice
  upo.practice_categories      applies? standing? evidence, next step
  upo.practice_metrics         this practice's value for a measure, with date and basis
  upo.risk_findings, recommendations, projects, worklist_items, valuations
blocks.caption: The shape of the framework. Indentation shows what belongs to what.

blocks.text: Two properties follow. The universal part and the practice part are separate, so the same 117 areas can be applied to any practice by adding rows for it. And every statement carries its source and a confidence label, so a reader can tell a regulation from a convention.

items: Edit a seed file, for example the file for one domain or the practice's work list.
Run the checker. It refuses unknown fields, broken references and anything that looks like patient information.
Load it into the preview copy of the database and look at the preview site.
Load it into production.

blocks.text:
python3 optimization/tools/upo_load.py validate
python3 optimization/tools/upo_load.py load --target preview
python3 optimization/tools/upo_load.py load --target prod
blocks.caption: The three commands. Work-list status and notes entered in the application are never overwritten by a load.

blocks.text: An agent here is a scheduled routine that reads, decides by rule, acts, and writes down what it did. One billing run does roughly this:

items: Read the new census and charges from the rounding tool.
Check each patient's coverage electronically. Flag changes.
Enter charges into the billing system and run its checks.
Send claims. Read back acknowledgments and rejections.
Read remittances, post payments, and classify every unpaid line by reason.
Apply standing rules: resend what can be fixed, queue what needs a person, write off what the rules allow.
Write a run record and update the database.

blocks.text: The rulebook is the important part. It is a written file of standing instructions from the owner, such as never billing care management to Medicaid. A rule is cheap to add and repeats perfectly, which is the strength and the danger.

blocks.title: Controls that belong around any billing agent
blocks.text: A person approves any rule that changes a code, a date, a place of service or a balance. Someone samples the agents' actions against charts every month. An outside coder reads the rulebook once a year. Every action is logged with the rule that caused it. The practice, not the software, is responsible for each claim.
The application is one small web service. It verifies who you are, checks your address against an approved list, records the request, and answers with data.

rows: This practice's assessment, scorecard, risks, plan, projects, work list and valuation
The purchased library with scores and checked claims
The only address that writes: it saves a status and a note with your name and the time

items: Sign-in is handled by a managed service. The application receives a signed token and checks the signature on every request.
Every request is written to an access log.
The service runs next to the database, and each copy of the database gets its own copy of the service, so changes are tried on a preview before production.

sections.heading: Turning this into something other practices can use

blocks.text: The pieces specific to one practice are fewer than they look.

rows: The 13 domains, 117 areas and their measures
Which areas apply and where the practice stands
Connections to that practice's billing system and bank
The loader, the checker, the mirror
The rulebook, because rules follow specialty, payers and state

items: Connect the data: billing system extracts, bank deposits, financial statements, public Medicare data for each clinician.
Compute the measures and compare with benchmarks and with national code patterns.
Judge each area: applies or not, standing, evidence, next step.
Write the risk review, the plan and the valuation.
Review everything with a certified coder and, where needed, an attorney before it reaches the owner.

blocks.title: What makes this a regulated activity
blocks.text: Handling another practice's patient data requires a business associate agreement and security safeguards. Advice about coding and billing carries liability. A service like this should be sold as management information with professional review, not as a guarantee of compliance or revenue.

takeaways: Five layers: sources, agents, one database, an interface, and a three-way mirror.
A claim is a standard message built from service codes, diagnoses, a place of service and identifiers. The remittance tells you why each dollar was not paid.
The framework is data: 13 domains, 117 areas and 186 measures as rows, each with a source.
Change content by editing a file, checking it, previewing it and loading it.
Agents repeat rules perfectly, so the rules need human approval, sampling and an outside read.
Universal content and practice content are stored separately, which is what would let the same system serve another practice.
